nature-acct-050.title: Life-cycle assessment: from cradle to grave
nature-acct-050.text: Every manufactured product has a life story. It begins when raw materials are extracted, the cradle, and runs through making, distribution and use to recycling or disposal, the grave. Life-cycle assessment, or LCA, adds up the environmental impacts of a product, process or service across every stage of that life. An LCA inventories the energy and materials needed across the supply chain and calculates the resulting emissions. It covers more than greenhouse gases, including water pollution, air pollution and ecotoxicity, harm to living things from toxic substances. At first LCA was used mainly to compare a product with alternatives. Now it informs product design, product labelling ({{ref:nature-pol-186}}), consumer education and government policy. An LCA is only as accurate as its data, which come either as unit process data or as environmental input-output data. Critics note that not every factor can be reduced to a number. Rigid system boundaries, the lines that decide what is counted, also make change hard to capture.

nature-clim-264.title: Emission intensity: pollution per unit of activity
nature-clim-264.text: Between 1978 and 2018 the carbon intensity of global energy fell 13%, from 66.3 to 58.0 kg of CO2 per gigajoule, mainly through more renewables and nuclear power. Emission intensity, also called carbon intensity, is the amount of a pollutant released per unit of an activity. Examples are grams of CO2 per megajoule of energy, or greenhouse gases per unit of GDP. Intensities let analysts estimate emissions from activity data such as fuel burned, animals kept or distances travelled. They also let people compare the environmental impact of different fuels or activities. Carbon intensity per kilowatt-hour is widely used to compare sources of electricity. Chemistry explains much of the difference. Coal, mostly carbon, has a high CO2 intensity; natural gas, with four hydrogen atoms per carbon, has a medium one. In Europe from 1990 to 2007, CO2 per unit of GDP fell 2.3% a year, faster than energy use per unit of GDP at 1.4% a year. Methods matter, though: a full life-cycle count and a combustion-only count can give different results.

nature-acct-047.title: Biocapacity: what nature can supply each year
nature-acct-047.text: In 2016 Earth had about 12.2 billion hectares of productive land and water. Divided among 7.4 billion people, that came to 1.6 hectares of average productivity each, and those 1.6 hectares also had to cover the space wild species need. That supply is biocapacity: an estimate of how much useful biological material an ecosystem can produce, and how much waste such as carbon dioxide it can absorb ({{ref:nature-found-020}}). It is the supply side against which human demand, the {{ref:nature-acct-027}}, is compared to measure human impact. An area's biocapacity is its physical area multiplied by a yield factor and an equivalence factor. It is not fixed. It changes with technology, since what counts as a useful material can change from year to year. Population growth can also lower biocapacity per person, since Earth's resources must be shared among more people.

nature-acct-027.title: Ecological footprint: how much planet a lifestyle needs
nature-acct-027.text: Global Footprint Network estimated humanity's footprint for 2023 at 1.71 planet Earths: people demanded 1.71 times what ecosystems renewed. The ecological footprint is the measure behind that figure. It counts how much nature, as biologically productive land and sea, people need to support their way of life and their economies. Footprint accounts compare that area with the productive area actually available, the biocapacity. Resource use of every kind is converted into standard land areas ({{ref:nature-acct-049}}). The footprint can be calculated for an activity, a person, a city, a nation or all of humanity, and split by category such as food, housing and goods. Humanity's footprint grew from 7.0 billion standard hectares in 1961 to 20.6 billion in 2014, driven by higher use per person and more people. Its fastest-growing part is carbon, about 60% of the total ({{ref:nature-acct-031}}). Per-person footprints range from 14.3 standard hectares in Qatar to just half a hectare in Yemen. {{ref:nature-hist-067}} developed the concept and method for his PhD in Vancouver from 1990 to 1994, supervised by William Rees, who coined the name.

nature-acct-031.title: Carbon footprint: one number for climate impact
nature-acct-031.text: The term first appeared in 1999, in a BBC vegetarian food magazine. A carbon footprint is the total amount of greenhouse gases that an activity, product, company or country adds to the atmosphere, expressed as one comparable number. It is usually reported in tonnes of CO2-equivalent per unit, such as per year, per kilogram of protein or per kilometre travelled. CO2-equivalent rolls all greenhouse gases, not only carbon dioxide, into one figure ({{ref:nature-eco-159}}). That single number lets people compare the climate impact of individuals, products, companies and countries, and set priorities for cutting it. The World Bank put the global average in 2014 at about 5 tonnes of CO2 per person, counted on a production basis. With 9–10 billion people by 2050, staying within a 2 °C target needs a footprint of about 2–2.5 tonnes CO2e per person. The single number has a cost. Focusing on carbon alone can lead people to ignore or worsen other harms, such as biodiversity loss and habitat destruction.

nature-acct-076.title: IUCN Red List: the world's register of threatened species
nature-acct-076.text: As of 2023, 42,108 of 150,388 species surveyed were considered at risk of extinction from human activity such as too much fishing, hunting and land development. The count comes from the IUCN Red List, the global inventory, founded in 1964, of the conservation status and extinction risk of the world's species ({{ref:nature-eco-087}}). Its goals are to report species' status, draw attention to threatened biodiversity, and influence policy and conservation action. The first two volumes, for mammals and birds, were published in 1966. Peer-reviewed specialist groups aim to re-evaluate every species at least every ten years. In 2012, 41% of amphibian species, 33% of reef-building corals, 25% of mammals and 13% of birds were threatened. A 2016 study argued its classification is inconsistent. Adding mapped location data, it found, would move many species to higher risk categories.

nature-acct-044.title: Water footprint: the hidden water in what people consume
nature-acct-044.text: The average person's water footprint is 1,385 cubic metres a year. Arjen Hoekstra coined the concept in 2002 as a consumption-based indicator, modelled on the ecological footprint of the 1990s. A water footprint is the total volume of fresh water used to produce the goods and services that a person, community or business consumes or produces. Water use counts as the volume evaporated or polluted per unit of time. Unlike traditional withdrawal statistics, it shows where water is used and polluted, not only how much. A product's footprint is the sum over all processes in its supply chain, divided by the number of units. Since July 2014, ISO 14046:2014 has given guidance for assessments based on life-cycle assessment principles. Critics note that a footprint means little without regional scarcity. The 140 litres behind a cup of coffee may be harmless in humid areas but damaging in arid ones.

nature-acct-056.title: Sustainability measurement: quantifying a slippery goal
nature-acct-056.text: Sustainability has no fixed definition, so measuring it is hard, perhaps impossible. Sustainability measurement is the set of frameworks and indicators that try anyway, for a process, product, service or business. Frameworks look at environmental, social and economic domains, with tools such as indicators, benchmarks and audits. A benchmark is a reference point for a measurement; once set, it allows trends and progress to be measured. The toolbox includes life-cycle assessment for resource use, the ecological footprint for consumption, and {{ref:nature-acct-069}} for governance. A UN commission published a list of 140 indicators covering environmental, social, economic and institutional aspects. Because each country uses its own indicators, global comparisons can be misread; common indexes would allow comparison.

nature-acct-080.title: Input–output models: how every industry feeds the others
nature-acct-080.text: In any economy, one sector's output becomes other sectors' inputs. An input–output model is a quantitative economic model that maps these dependencies. It is laid out as a matrix, a grid of numbers, usually in money. Columns show the inputs each sector buys; rows show the outputs it sells. Wassily Leontief developed it and won the Nobel Prize in Economics for it; a cruder forerunner was Quesnay's table of the economy ({{ref:nature-hist-018}}). Statistics offices use it in national accounts, including to calculate GDP. It is increasingly used to measure environmental footprints for consumption-based accounting, such as tracing the carbon embodied in goods traded between economies. Being linear, built from simple proportions, it is cheap to compute. But it needs huge amounts of data, so tables are often published 5–7 years late. And because tables are in money, every dollar spent in a sector is assumed to cause the same damage, which can bias environmental estimates.

nature-acct-070.title: Environmental indicators: simple numbers for a complex world
nature-acct-070.text: People respond best to clear, simple measures, such as the UV index and the air quality index. That is the logic of the environmental indicator: a simple measure, tracked over time, that tells what is happening in the environment. Indicators are a practical, cheaper way to follow a complex environment than recording every variable. The concentration of ozone-depleting substances in the air, for example, indicates the state of ozone depletion in the stratosphere. The OECD's Pressure-State-Response model sorts indicators into three kinds. Pressure indicators include greenhouse gas emissions. State indicators describe the condition of the environment. Response indicators include the number of people served by sewage treatment. Good indicators are judged on scientific credibility, policy relevance and practical data needs. Environmental indicators are a subset of broader indicators of development that also cover social and economic health. Large sets are condensed into indices, headline indicators, traffic-light visuals or dashboards.

nature-acct-061.title: Embedded emissions: the carbon hidden in trade
nature-acct-061.text: In 2004, 23% of global emissions were embedded in internationally traded goods. They flowed mostly from China and developing countries to the US, Europe and Japan. Embedded emissions, also called embodied emissions or embodied carbon, are the greenhouse gases released in making a good, counted as belonging to whoever consumes it. Emissions are usually counted where they are produced, as countries do when reporting under the UN climate convention ({{ref:nature-clim-053}}). So emissions embedded in imports are attributed to the exporting country. Wang and Watson suggested in 2007 that nearly a quarter of China's CO2 emissions might come from producing exports. In Western Europe, imported emissions make up 20-50% of consumed emissions. Choosing between production and consumption accounting is partly a question of fairness: who is responsible for emissions? One response is {{ref:nature-pol-265}}, a tariff on the carbon embedded in imports.

nature-acct-043.title: Earth Overshoot Day: when the year's budget runs out
nature-acct-043.text: In 2024, Earth Overshoot Day fell on August 1. From then on, humanity was using more than Earth could regenerate in that whole year. The date equals world biocapacity divided by world ecological footprint, multiplied by the 365 days of the year. In economic terms it is the day the planet's yearly regenerative budget is spent and humanity starts deficit spending. Andrew Simms of the New Economics Foundation developed the idea, and Global Footprint Network calculates it. Human consumption began to outstrip what the planet could reproduce in the early 1970s. In 2020 coronavirus lockdowns pushed the date to 22 August, more than three weeks later than in 2019. Critics say it mainly reflects excess carbon dioxide and measures poor management of land and water badly. The Breakthrough Institute called it a publicity stunt, and Global Footprint Network researchers published a response.

nature-acct-033.title: Consumption-based accounting: charging emissions to the buyer
nature-acct-033.text: Developed countries' emissions appear to be falling. Count trade, and a 2% decrease under production accounting becomes a 7% increase. Consumption-based emission accounting assigns all the emissions along a global supply chain to the place where the goods are finally consumed. Its opposite, production-based or territorial accounting, counts only emissions released inside a country; it is what countries report under the UN climate convention. Because it includes the emissions behind imported goods and services, consumption-based accounting is more comprehensive. It also reflects the lifestyle choices of a country's citizens. It rests on input-output analysis, extended worldwide as multi-regional input-output analysis, or MRIO. It is more complex and uncertain, since it needs an extra step and data from every trading partner. Some suggest using it as a 'shadow' to production accounts.

nature-clim-164.title: Scope 1, 2 and 3: sorting a company's emissions
nature-clim-164.text: Oil companies that claim net-zero operations leave out their customers burning the oil, which is 70–90% of oil-related emissions. Those emissions fall in Scope 3. {{ref:nature-gov-109}} splits an organization's emissions three ways. Scope 1 covers direct emissions from sources it owns or controls, such as fuel burned on site. For a person, that means a car or a gas stove. Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat, cooling or steam. Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions from sources the organization does not own or control, including suppliers and the users of its products. Scope 3 can dwarf the others: it made up 75% of emissions reported to the Carbon Disclosure Project. Yet in 2022 only about 30% of US companies reported it. Footprints that leave out Scope 3 can mislead customers about the real footprint of companies or products.

nature-acct-051.title: The four phases of a life-cycle assessment
nature-acct-051.text: The ISO 14040 and 14044 standards set out a life-cycle assessment in four phases. First, goal and scope fix the product's function, the functional unit it is measured by, the system boundaries, assumptions and allocation rules. Second, the life cycle inventory, or LCI, quantifies raw material and energy needs and all emissions and releases over the product's life. Third, the life cycle impact assessment, or LCIA, evaluates the potential environmental and human health impacts of those flows. Fourth, interpretation summarizes the results and ends in conclusions and recommendations. The phases depend on one another, so no stage counts as final until the whole study is done.

nature-acct-060.title: Ecological indicators: counting beetles to judge a field
nature-acct-060.text: The number of beetle taxa, or kinds, in a field can indicate its biodiversity. That is an ecological indicator. It sums up the state of an ecosystem, or the human impact on it, in simple terms for the public and policy makers. Such indicators save cost and time. Instead of counting every bird and plant in a restored wetland, a few indicator species can be monitored. They are a subset of environmental indicators that refer only to ecological processes. Their limits include patchy data, no international standards, missing reference levels, and neglect of hard-to-measure values such as beauty.

nature-acct-055.title: Living Planet Index: tracking the world's wildlife
nature-acct-055.text: Between 1970 and 2020, monitored wildlife populations fell by an average of 73%, the 2024 report showed. In Latin America and the Caribbean declines averaged 94%, with land-use change and habitat loss a key driver ({{ref:nature-res-108}}). The Living Planet Index tracks global biodiversity through the population trends of vertebrates, animals with backbones, around the world. WWF developed it in 1997 with UNEP-WCMC; since 2006 the Zoological Society of London has managed it with WWF. As of 2022 it drew on 31,821 populations of 5,230 species of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish. It is limited to vertebrates because long-term data for invertebrates and plants are scarcer. It was used to measure progress toward a global biodiversity target for 2010 and the later {{ref:nature-gov-017}}. Media often wrongly report it as showing that 69% of all animals or species were lost since 1970. Researchers also dispute whether it reflects true changes in abundance. Some studies find it sensitive to outliers and biased by its mathematics, possibly overstating declines; others contest those re-analyses.

nature-acct-077.title: Red List categories: from Least Concern to Extinct
nature-acct-077.text: The IUCN Red List sorts species into nine groups, from Extinct to Not Evaluated. Placement depends on criteria such as rate of decline, population size and range. Extinct means that, beyond reasonable doubt, the species is no longer alive. Extinct in the Wild means it survives only in captivity or cultivation. Next come the three categories grouped as 'threatened': Critically Endangered, Endangered and Vulnerable. Near Threatened, Least Concern, Data Deficient and Not Evaluated complete the scheme. All new assessments since 2001 use version 3.1 of the categories and criteria.

nature-acct-086.title: Red List Index: watching extinction risk change over time
nature-acct-086.text: Australia's national bird index fell from 0.927 in 1990 to 0.896 in 2020, picking up both the 2019–2020 wildfires and conservation successes. That is a Red List Index, or RLI. Built from the IUCN Red List, it tracks how the extinction risk of whole groups of species changes over time. Repeating assessments at regular intervals lets changes in threat status reveal trends. The index can be broken down by taxonomic group, biogeographic realm, habitat type or main threat. Assessing every fungus, insect and plant is impractical, so a sampled version, the SRLI, assesses a representative sample. The shark and ray index has fallen 19% since the 1970s because of too much fishing. The RLI is the single indicator for target 15.5 of the {{ref:nature-gov-010}}, and was used for the 2010 global biodiversity target.

nature-acct-078.title: Red List of Ecosystems: rating the risk of collapse
nature-acct-078.text: Whole ecosystems, not only species, can disappear. The IUCN Red List of Ecosystems is the global framework for assessing how close ecosystems are to collapse, the ecosystem-level counterpart of the Red List of species. It replaced national protocols that were often not comparable. The IUCN began developing it in 2008, finalized its categories and criteria in 2013 and officially recognized it in 2014. It aims to evaluate all the world's ecosystems by 2025, to help focus limited conservation effort on those most likely to disappear. Some countries, such as Finland, have adopted it as their official system. Its concepts are debated. Critics point to the lack of a consistent way to classify ecosystems and to argument over what ecosystem collapse means.

nature-acct-037.title: Sustainability metrics and indices: many yardsticks, no standard
nature-acct-037.text: There is no universal standard for measuring sustainability, so disciplines and international organizations have proposed many different indicators. Sustainability metrics and indices are numerical measures that try to quantify sustainability's environmental, social and economic sides. Examples include the ecological footprint, the Human Development Index, the Genuine Progress Index and {{ref:nature-acct-042}}. Such aggregate measures give a more detailed view of development than traditional indicators such as GDP. Interest in index systems has expanded since the 2010s, more in industrialized than developing countries. Yet for all their popularity, these measures often have limited effect on actual policy and practice.

nature-acct-045.title: Blue, green and grey water: three shades of a footprint
nature-acct-045.text: Nearly all the water behind beef is rain. Green water has been estimated at 94% of the water footprint of global beef cattle production. A water footprint has three parts, each named by a colour. A blue footprint counts water taken from lakes, rivers, wetlands and underground water stores ({{ref:nature-res-112}}) that evaporates, enters a product, or is returned elsewhere or later. A green footprint counts rain stored in the soil's root zone that plants transpire or take up; it matters most for farm and forest goods. A grey footprint is the water needed to dilute pollutants until the water meets agreed quality standards. That last part draws criticism. Critics say the grey footprint treats pollution like scarcity, though the two affect people and nature differently.

nature-acct-057.title: Sustainability indicators: simple questions for policy
nature-acct-057.text: Indicator sets answer simple questions. What is happening? Are targets being reached? Are things improving? A sustainability indicator tracks some part of the interplay between the environment and social and economic activity. Descriptive indicators say what is happening; performance indicators say whether targets are being met. They are scientific constructs whose principal purpose is to inform public policy-making. They can cover the environment, society or the economy, but there is no fixed definition of a sustainability indicator.

nature-acct-071.title: Environmentally extended input–output analysis: tracing impacts through trade
nature-acct-071.text: As trade makes global resource use more important, accounts must follow emissions from producer to final buyer. Environmentally extended input–output analysis, or EEIO, is the main way such consumption-based accounts are compiled. It attaches resource use and emissions to an economy's input–output tables, so they can be traced through production to final consumption. Each industry's extra inputs, such as energy, materials and labour, and its outputs, such as emissions, are added as an extension matrix of factors per unit of output. Multiplying final demand by {{ref:nature-acct-081}} and these factors allocates resource use and emissions to domestic or export demand. National tables are combined into multi-regional input–output models, or MRIO, to reflect differing production structures. The method assumes each industry makes one uniform product at one price, which aggregation and by-products violate. It also assumes constant returns to scale, where doubling inputs doubles output, an assumption shared by life-cycle assessment.

openers.footprints-and-indicators: Every product has a history of energy, water and emissions behind it, and every person and country draws on nature to live. This chapter is about the tools that make that demand visible. {{ref:nature-acct-050}} adds up a product's impacts from raw materials to disposal. {{ref:nature-acct-027}}, {{ref:nature-acct-031}} and {{ref:nature-acct-044}} each turn a way of life into a comparable number, to be set against what ecosystems can supply, their {{ref:nature-acct-047}}. Indicators such as {{ref:nature-acct-076}} track the state of nature itself, and {{ref:nature-acct-043}} marks the date each year when humanity's use of resources passes what Earth can regenerate.

reviews.footprints-and-indicators: The tools in this chapter turn human demand on nature into numbers that can be compared. Life-cycle assessment and input–output analysis trace impacts through supply chains, from a single product to whole economies, and reveal how much carbon is embedded in trade. Footprints then set demand against supply: humanity's ecological footprint ran at 1.71 Earths in 2023, which is why Earth Overshoot Day falls before the year is out. Indicators such as the Living Planet Index and the Red Lists record the result in nature itself. Every tool has blind spots too, from the money-based assumptions of input–output tables to critics who say the footprint mostly measures carbon.
